vision_features.image_context: Close-up view of a soybean plant at or near ground level. Multiple stems and pods are visible. The image shows the lower portion of the plant with stems, dried/maturing pods, and surrounding soil and plant debris. Both green stems and dried plant material are present.
vision_features.abnormalities: 1. Pods: The pods visible throughout the image are notably flat and shriveled, appearing largely empty or containing underdeveloped seeds. They are elongated (approximately 20-30mm long), tan to light golden-brown in color, with a papery, dry texture. The pods appear deflated rather than plump and rounded as would be expected in fully developed pods. They are distributed across multiple branches throughout the image. Some pods appear to have fine tan/brown hairs on their surface. 2. Stems in the lower portion: The stems near the base of the plant show some discoloration — transitioning from green in the upper portions to a slightly grayish-green or dull green near the soil level. One stem near the base appears to have a slightly darkened, grayish segment approximately 10-15mm in length. 3. Surrounding plant material: There is a significant amount of dry, brown, collapsed plant debris at the base — including what appear to be older dried leaves and stems — lying on the dark soil surface.
vision_features.absences: 1. No plump, seed-filled pods are visible — pods that would normally be round and bulging with developed seeds are absent. 2. No green leaves are visible anywhere on the plant — all foliar tissue appears to have already dropped or dried. 3. No visible powdery coating, sticky residue, or thread-like growth on the stem surfaces. 4. No raised, colored pustules or dots visible on the pod or stem surfaces.
vision_features.summary: The image shows a soybean plant in late season, with green stems still present but all pods appearing flat, papery, and empty or poorly filled — tan to golden-brown in color and shriveled in appearance. No leaves remain on the plant. The most striking feature is the near-total absence of seed fill in the pods, which hang deflated along the stems. The pods are the most severely affected organ. The contrast between the still-green stems and the completely dried, empty pods is the most unusual visual characteristic.

Knowledge-base entry for 'Green_stem_disorder':
────────────────────────────────────────
All or part of the soybean plant remains green while the rest of the plant or neighboring plants mature, most commonly seen in stems, leaves or pods; stems remain moist while pods and seeds have ripened.. Stems and occasionally leaves remain green and moist after pods and seeds have ripened and turned brown; excessive leaves on plant and green stems when neighboring plants are near harvest maturity.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Diaporthe':
────────────────────────────────────────
Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped specks or pycnidia on mature soybean stems occurring later in the season (R6 to R8 growth stages). Pycnidia may also develop on dry, poorly developed pods, but may be dispersed randomly rather than arranged linearly.. Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped pycnidia arranged linearly on stems; random dispersal on pods.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phomopsis':
────────────────────────────────────────
Infected seed are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may have a gray mold on them.. Seed infected by pod and stem blight may decompose after harvest and have low viability; seedlings grown from infected seeds may often be blighted.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phytophthora':
────────────────────────────────────────
Young plants show rapid yellowing and wilting with soft rot and collapse of the root. Mature plants exhibit general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, followed by wilting and death, with brown discolored roots and a dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes; leaves typically stay attached after plant death.. The best diagnostic symptom on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration (dark chocolate-brown) that may extend several nodes up the stem. Root system shows lateral and branch roots almost completely discolored; tap roots with brown surface discoloration and tan to brown inner tissue discoloration. Leaves turn yellow, wilt, and typically stay attached after plant death.. stem canker, Pythium
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Bacterial_Blight':
────────────────────────────────────────
Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies. Lesions have dark reddish-brown centers surrounded by yellowish-green halos around water-soaked tissue; lesions may coalesce to form large, irregularly shaped lesions. Leaf veins may become affected creating necrotic areas resembling lightning on the leaf. Eventually lesions fall out leaving ragged foliage.. Presence of a yellowish-green halo around lesions; most common on young leaves in mid to upper canopy whereas brown spot is usually seen on older, lower leaves; lack of fungal structures in lesions.. Septoria brown spot, brown spot
────────────────────────────────────────

DISCRIMINATING: 'Green_stem_disorder' vs 'Diaporthe'
Ruling feature : Presence of black, flask-shaped pycnidia (specks) on stems vs. abnormal green/moist tissue retention
Green_stem_disorder: Stems and leaves remain green and moist after pods and seeds have ripened and turned brown; excessive foliage while neighboring plants are near harvest maturity.
Diaporthe: Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped pycnidia (pycnidia) arranged linearly on mature, dry stems; pycnidia may also appear randomly on dry, poorly developed pods.
Decision rule  : IF the stems show distinct black, flask-shaped specks arranged in parallel rows, THEN it is Diaporthe; IF the stems remain green and moist while pods/seeds have already ripened and browned, THEN it is Green Stem Disorder.

DISCRIMINATING: 'Green_stem_disorder' vs 'Phytophthora'
Ruling feature : Stem color and moisture: green/moist vs. dark chocolate-brown discoloration
Green_stem_disorder: Stems remain green and moist even after pods and seeds have ripened and turned brown; excessive green leaves persist while neighboring plants approach harvest maturity.
Phytophthora: Stems show a dark chocolate-brown discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes; leaves yellow, wilt, and remain attached after plant death.
Decision rule  : IF the stem is green and moist with ripened pods/seeds present, suspect Green Stem Disorder (A); IF the lower stem shows dark chocolate-brown discoloration extending upward from the soil line with yellowing/wilted leaves that stay attached, suspect Phytophthora (B).

DISCRIMINATING: 'Green_stem_disorder' vs 'Phomopsis'
Ruling feature : Green, moist stems vs. cracked, shriveled, moldy seeds
Green_stem_disorder: Stems and leaves remain green and moist while pods and seeds have already ripened and turned brown; plant retains excessive green tissue when neighboring plants are near harvest maturity.
Phomopsis: Seeds are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may be covered with gray mold; infected seeds may decompose after harvest and produce blighted seedlings.
Decision rule  : IF the plant shows green, moist stems and leaves persisting after pods/seeds have ripened, THEN suspect Green Stem Disorder; IF the seeds themselves appear cracked, shriveled, dull, or have gray mold, THEN suspect Phomopsis.
